title: Create your first plugin from the template
breadcrumb: Create your first plugin from the template

blocks.html:
The fastest, most reliable way to start is to copy the helloworld example (or the leaner plugintemplate) and rename it. Both already contain the manifest, the plugin.xml, the four plumbing classes, and a working Gradle build.

Project layout

A plugin is a standard single-module Android Gradle project:

helloworld/
├── build.gradle            # top-level: SDK location, takdev plugin, repos
├── settings.gradle         # include ':app'
├── gradle.properties       # android.useAndroidX=true, enableR8=false
├── gradlew / gradlew.bat
└── app/
    ├── build.gradle        # the plugin module: flavors, signing, deps
    ├── proguard-gradle.txt
    └── src/main/
        ├── AndroidManifest.xml
        ├── assets/
        │   └── plugin.xml   # declares the IPlugin entry point (ATAK 5.x)
        ├── java/com/atakmap/android/helloworld/
        │   ├── plugin/
        │   │   ├── HelloWorldLifecycle.java   # entry point (extends AbstractPlugin)
        │   │   └── HelloWorldTool.java        # toolbar button
        │   ├── HelloWorldMapComponent.java    # functionality
        │   └── HelloWorldDropDownReceiver.java# UI panel
        └── res/             # layouts, drawables, strings

By convention the two entry-point classes live in a …/plugin/ sub-package, separate from your feature code, purely for readability.

Rename it to your plugin

When you copy the template, change these in lockstep so nothing collides with the example or with other installed plugins:

  1. **rootProject.name** in settings.gradle (this also names your output APK).
  2. The Java package (com.atakmap.android.helloworld → your own), and the matching **namespace** in app/build.gradle. (In ATAK 5.x the package lives in the namespace property, not as a package="…" attribute in the manifest.)
  3. The class names (HelloWorld* → YourPlugin*) and the impl reference in plugin.xml.
  4. The broadcast action string that opens your panel (the example uses com.atakmap.android.helloworld.SHOW_HELLO_WORLD) — give it your own namespace.
  5. app_name / app_desc in res/values/strings.xml, and the launcher icon.

The manifest, piece by piece

AndroidManifest.xml does three plugin-specific jobs (everything else is ordinary Android):

<application ... android:icon="@drawable/ic_launcher" android:label="@string/app_name">

    <!-- 1. Which ATAK API this plugin targets (filled by the build flavor) -->
    <meta-data android:name="plugin-api" android:value="${atakApiVersion}"/>
    <meta-data android:name="app_desc"   android:value="@string/app_desc"/>

    <!-- 2. Any services/activities your plugin needs are normal Android components -->

    <!-- 3. The discovery hook that makes ATAK treat this APK as a plugin -->
    <activity android:name="com.atakmap.app.component"
        tools:ignore="MissingClass">
        <intent-filter android:label="@string/app_name">
            <action android:name="com.atakmap.app.component" />
        </intent-filter>
    </activity>
</application>

You do not implement a class for com.atakmap.app.component — the tools:ignore attribute is there precisely because the class lives in ATAK, not your APK. It is only a discovery marker.

The plugin.xml wiring

app/src/main/assets/plugin.xml is what actually connects your code to ATAK. In ATAK 5.x it declares a single extension — your plugin entry point, of type gov.tak.api.plugin.IPlugin:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<!-- if you change this file, make sure to tick the versionCode in AndroidManifest. -->
<plugin>
    <extension
        type="gov.tak.api.plugin.IPlugin"
        impl="com.atakmap.android.helloworld.plugin.HelloWorldLifecycle"
        singleton="true" />
</plugin>

Point the impl at your renamed entry-point class. That's the whole contract: ATAK reads plugin.xml and instantiates your entry point (an AbstractPlugin), which in turn registers your toolbar button and your functionality — covered next.

With the skeleton renamed and wired, the next step is to understand what those two classes do.
